This may not be standard advice, but I would recommend buying an older (1960s or before) US made non-plastic machine--I have a Singer from 1939 and the thing is built like a tank. They are simple as heck. No electronics, no nothing that you can't repair, just oil it occasionally and replace the power cord if it looks old. I had a repairman come over and work it over for $75 (the machine was $80 but I'm in CA and it came with the attachments for making buttonholes and such) and it has never given any trouble these past 6 years. There are plenty of Youtube videos on the mechanics of these machines and they are easily figured out. They are really fun to use too.

I was hesitant to put down a used machine. I have one from the 60s I won’t dare get rid of, but it came at a cost. My dad bought it for me not knowing much about sewing machines. $120 later I finally got it to work correctly.

Along this same line of thinking, I acquired my cousin's machine (A Janome "New Home"), which previously belonged to my aunt, and was bought in the 70s. It's metal, heavy, and an absolutely lovely beast of a machine. I love it.

Before dropping bank on a machine, go around and ask some of the ladies from your family if they have one gathering dust in the closet. They probably do, everybody had one back then. You might need to take it in to get a tune up (the shop near me starts at $75) and a possible repair. In the end, you'd be spending about the same amount and ending up with an ultimately better quality sewing machine. Every time I go to JoAnn Fabrics and look at what they have available, I just keep walking because what I have is better, even if it's not as automated.
